body:
# Memory Beads
**Document status.** This document is a feature proposal. It defines the desired product behavior, capabilities, and architectural boundaries for Memory Beads. It is not an implementation plan.

**Revision 3 — 2026-08-31.** Applies the follow-up review round — archive collapsed into deletion-with-history, erasure separated from it, R27a, and the derivation-field refinements — with each change and its reason in the accompanying change-list comment.

**Revision 2 — 2026-08-31.** Applies the decisions recorded in the review thread; the change-list comment accompanying this revision enumerates every edit and its source.
## Summary
Beads already has a small memory feature: `bd remember` stores a string under a key, `bd recall` reads it, `bd memories` lists or searches the key/value set, and `bd forget` removes a found non-empty entry. Out-of-band empty rows survive `forget` and require recovery. `bd prime` can inject memory bodies at session start. This is useful for a few reminders, but the storage model has no canonical Bead identity, no history reachable through the memory commands, no structured change authorship, no per-memory version identity, no explicit links, no way to remove a memory without losing its record, and no way for a task to cite the exact knowledge it used.

The gap shows up whenever project knowledge matters for more than one session. A corrected policy can silently replace the only copy of the old policy. A task cannot identify the exact historical state it was written against. Humans and agents cannot inspect how a decision changed or who changed it. At startup, loading every remembered body spends context before the agent knows what it needs.

The usual workaround is a collection of Markdown files, task descriptions, agent-specific memory files, and conventions about where to look. Those files can be good documents, but every tool assembles them differently. Knowledge gets duplicated, the task graph cannot cite it structurally, and a fresh agent has to rediscover the project's filing system before doing the work.

Task Beads already give project work an identity that outlasts any one agent session. Memory Beads expand the Beads core so durable project knowledge is a first-class Bead kind beside Task Beads. A Memory Bead has canonical identity, Markdown content, participation in shared Beads History with Change Attribution, deletion that keeps history, restoration, and explicit relationships to tasks and other memories. Retrieval starts with compact search or a task's references, followed by an explicit complete read. The existing memory commands keep working, with their canonical and compatibility meanings defined in R25.

The current `memoryops.Memories` [contract](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/e29abaea376b30982721e2446676e66b7db2e8b0/memoryops/memories.go#L126-L198) and `bd` [memory commands](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/e29abaea376b30982721e2446676e66b7db2e8b0/cmd/bd/memory.go#L236-L496) establish the existing keyed-memory behavior and public entry points. They are implementation evidence for the compatibility baseline, not definitions of the target's internal APIs or storage mechanisms.

* * *
## Goals
### Let the project remember
A new human or agent should be able to start from a task, find the knowledge that matters, read only what it chooses, and identify the exact historical Memory states it used. When knowledge changes, another person can inspect and compare retained history, see Change Attribution, make a deliberate correction under the common Versioned Bead rules, and retire the knowledge without losing its record.

The record stays useful outside an agent session. A human can read the same Markdown, review changes, follow links, and build a handbook or wiki view over the graph. Beads stores what its callers deliberately record. It does not manufacture durable memory from prompts, transcripts, tool activity, or a failed search.
### Put work and knowledge in one core graph
Memory Beads extends Beads' core domain as a first-class Bead kind beside Task Beads. Memory identity, lifecycle, retrieval, and content semantics belong to the core Memory model. Versioning, historical addressing, writes, retries, concurrent editing, and conflicts come from shared Beads capabilities.

Bead References connect tasks to memories and memories to other memories without turning knowledge into workflow.

* * *
## Core model
- A **Memory Bead** is a first-class Bead containing durable Markdown knowledge. It exists or has been deleted — a deleted Memory has no current state while its retained versions stay addressable — and it never becomes ready, blocked, claimed, completed, or closed. Its durable state includes its title, body, optional key and aliases, outgoing references, metadata, derivation record, and Inception. It has no workflow-state dimension: versions of its durable state are its only change model.
  
- **Beads History** is the shared, provider-neutral Beads capability for observing, comparing, attributing, and addressing change over time. Memory Beads requires this capability but does not define its identifiers, branches, retention, storage, concurrency, or conflict mechanics.
  
- A **Versioned Bead** is a Bead whose durable state participates in Beads History. Memory Beads require that shared capability: a durable Memory change creates a version, while an unchanged Memory does not. An accepted version is **immutable**: its state never changes, a correction is a new version, and a removal leaves the version's address answering gone with the reason rather than resolving to anything else. Participation and behavior for other Bead kinds belong to their own contracts.
  
- **Change Attribution** is shared Beads History metadata identifying who or what was responsible for an accepted version and the available change context. It is not editable Memory state and does not turn an otherwise unchanged request into a change. **Inception** is editable origin or transfer metadata within a Memory Bead, such as whether its current state was created natively, converted, or imported; changing it changes durable Memory state. Application-specific properties live in `metadata`, never the body (R3).
  
- A **Bead Reference** is an explicit directional relationship; `related` is the built-in baseline type and the vocabulary is open (R17). Every Bead Reference carries a version, implicitly or explicitly: a specific version ID, or the well-known ID meaning **latest** — the default when none is stated. A reference whose version is a specific version ID is **pinned** — a **Historical Bead Reference** — and identifies one exact retained state of one Versioned Bead under the addressing model Beads History defines; that meaning does not imply the provider can reconstruct an entire historical project snapshot. The uses defined here have at least one Memory endpoint. A Bead Reference is informational, carries no instructions or authority, and never affects readiness.
  
- A **context consumer** is an application such as MindSpec that selects Beads and other project artifacts, assembles task context, and records what it used. It consumes Memory Beads but owns its artifact types, budgets, ordering, hashes, and receipts.
  

* * *
## User scenarios
### Remembering and maintaining knowledge
S1. Record durable knowledge without inventing a name

A developer records why the project avoids a tempting dependency. They supply a Markdown body but no title or key. Beads derives a short title, creates a Memory Bead with a canonical ID and first attributed version, and does not invent a key. A human may add or rename a familiar key later; former keys remain aliases, while agents can continue using the canonical ID.

S2. Search before writing and improve the existing memory

An agent is asked to preserve a newly discovered release convention. It searches compact memory results and finds an existing convention that already covers the subject. It recalls the complete body and updates that same Memory Bead using the common write rules for Versioned Beads rather than leaving a duplicate. An external quality tool may flag a possible duplicate or stale statement, but Beads does not decide that itself.

S3. Retire knowledge without losing the record

A workaround is no longer current. A maintainer forgets its Memory Bead. It disappears from current state and from search, but its retained versions and their Change Attribution remain readable by version according to the project's retention policy, pinned references to it still resolve, and a reference following `latest` reports that the target was deleted. If the workaround becomes relevant again, restoring it revives the same identity from a retained version rather than creating a replacement.
### Recalling and assembling context
S4. A fresh agent recalls only what it needs

A fresh supported coding agent starts from generated Beads guidance. It searches compact summaries, selects two plausible memories, recalls their complete bodies, and reports the Bead IDs and Historical Bead References that informed its work. `bd prime`, task loading, and search results do not inject unrelated memory bodies.

S5. A task cites the policy it depends on

A task has a Bead Reference to a security policy. Its structured record exposes the target identity and optional Historical Bead Reference without loading the target body. The task body explains why the policy matters. The executing agent explicitly recalls it before acting, and an exact historical reference continues to identify the same retained policy state after the policy changes.

S6. MindSpec builds a deterministic context pack

A [MindSpec-like context consumer](https://github.com/mrmaxsteel/mindspec/blob/09f62bd97b28bae7b171054066117cb19a33874d/.mindspec/core/ARCHITECTURE.md) reads a task's structured record, follows selected Bead References, and recalls exact historical Memory states. It combines those records with its own specs, ADRs, domain documents, and source files under a deterministic token policy. The resulting receipt identifies or hashes every input and explains why each was included. Beads makes each selected Memory's canonical identity, exact content, and Change Attribution available together; MindSpec decides which of those facts to record and owns the taxonomy, ordering, token tiers, file handling, and receipt format. Its pinned [context-pack budgeter specification](https://github.com/mrmaxsteel/mindspec/blob/09f62bd97b28bae7b171054066117cb19a33874d/.mindspec/specs/088-context-pack-budgeter/spec.md#L246-L355) documents its consumer-owned ordering, budgeting, input hashing, and receipt behavior.
### Versioning and integrity
S7. Two writers do not silently overwrite each other

Two people edit the same Memory Bead. Their writes follow the common Versioned Bead rules, so one cannot silently overwrite the other. After resolving the concurrent change through those shared rules, retained history and comparison show what changed and its Change Attribution.
### Linking knowledge to work
S8. A task and a memory link without changing workflow

A task links to the project's release policy, and that Memory Bead links to a supporting design rationale. Both links are explicit, directional, and non-blocking. The task keeps its existing dependency and readiness behavior, the source body explains why the reference matters, and neither task display nor reference traversal loads the target body. A caller can later remove either relationship with `bd unlink <source> <target>`; removing an outgoing Memory reference versions that source Memory without changing the target.

S9. A referenced target changes state

A task refers to the current release policy, and a Memory Bead refers to a supporting task. The policy or the supporting task is later deleted. Each surviving source keeps the stored reference without being revised merely because the target changed. Inspection reports the target's observed state without changing task readiness or silently retargeting the link.

S10. An exact historical reference does not drift

A reference whose version is `latest` follows the Memory Bead's current state. A pinned reference continues to identify the same retained state after the target changes: it resolves to exactly that state or to a typed refusal, never to a different one — a pinned reference can be superseded by newer versions of its target, but what it names never changes. Outgoing views for an exact historical state remain bound to that state, and a bounded incoming-reference view reports whether it is complete.
### Compatibility and interchange
S11. Existing key/value memory converts without silent loss

Converting legacy key/value memory to canonical Memory Beads preserves keys, bodies, and any history or Inception that can be represented truthfully. A legacy key with an empty value becomes a Memory with that key, a title derived from it, and an empty body. The accepted conversion change receives ordinary Change Attribution, while missing legacy authorship is disclosed rather than invented. Ambiguity, collisions, corruption, or another credible loss risk produces an actionable failure rather than false success, partial visibility, or invented evidence. If conversion is interrupted, callers see the still-usable legacy view, the complete canonical view, or an inspectable unavailable state that can be retried or recovered; they never receive an unexplained mixed view.

S12. Familiar commands map onto canonical Memory Beads

Existing users keep `bd remember`, `bd memories`, `bd recall`, and `bd forget`, but their target meanings are unambiguous. `remember` writes, canonical memories need no key, `forget` deletes without erasing history, structured discovery uses Bead IDs and compact records, and `prime` teaches selective retrieval instead of injecting bodies. Existing `bd memories --json` callers continue to receive the human-key-to-complete-body map, while keyed Go and HTTP interfaces remain compatibility projections of the same canonical Memory Beads. Canonical ID-based discovery is a separate structured representation that also supports unkeyed memories. `bd remember release-policy` writes a Memory whose body is `release-policy`; reading a Memory uses `bd recall`.

S13. Memory participates safely in shared interchange

A team transfers a selected graph containing tasks, memories, and their references through the shared Beads interchange facility. The destination either preserves the selected Memory state and reference meaning or rejects the transfer without a partial connected graph. A Memory is never identified or retargeted merely because a human key or similar-looking ID matches.
### Ecosystem use
S14. A viewer and a quality tool use the same public records

A viewer renders memory summaries, complete current and retained historical state, existence or deletion, references, comparisons, and Change Attribution without reading provider tables. A separate quality tool examines the same structured data for possible staleness, contradiction, duplication, or weak evidence. Beads preserves the material and exposes shared history capabilities; the tool makes the judgment.
### Change over time
S15. Temporary knowledge carries its own validity

A developer records a workaround that is only valid until a dependency ships its fix, and records that validity window in the Memory's metadata at write time. Beads moves nothing on a clock: consumers that care filter on the window, and when the fix ships the developer forgets the Memory. If the fix slips, the developer changes the window with an ordinary attributed edit; if the workaround is needed again after being forgotten, restoring it revives the same identity from its retained history.

S16. An application uses Beads History to update its own representation of memories

An application queries ordinary Beads History for all Bead changes from the position it last processed — or from a chosen instant on a first read — selects the Memory Bead changes, including removals of retained versions with their reasons, and reads the affected Memories through their public structured interfaces. The application decides how to synchronize those changes into Obsidian or any other application-specific representation. Beads does not own that synchronization process.

* * *
## Requirements
### Memory model and authoring
**R1. Memory is a first-class core Bead kind.** This feature intentionally expands the Beads charter from project work alone to peer core concepts for project work and durable project knowledge. A Memory Bead uses `type: "memory"`, participates in the Bead graph, and exists beside Task Beads rather than beneath the task model. Readiness, assignment, priority, claiming, completion, closure, and workflow dependencies do not apply to it. Queries and mutations whose meaning requires Task workflow state do not select or affect a Memory, and a workflow mutation addressed to one fails with a typed error. Generic Bead operations such as listing by kind, showing identity, and graph traversal can include Memory Beads. _(S1, S3)_

**R2. Canonical identity does not depend on a human key.** Every Memory Bead has a canonical Bead ID, owning Project ID, and supplied or derived title. A Memory Key is optional metadata and a selector. An application may encode prefixes, paths, or other structure in a key, but Beads treats the complete value as one opaque selector and assigns no meaning to its segments. Renaming one retains the former key as a visible alias. Current keys and aliases share one project-wide uniqueness namespace; deleting a Memory releases them, and an ordinary attributed rename or key removal frees a name from a live one. Canonical Bead ID wins positional ambiguity, while explicit selectors choose ID or key lookup. Unkeyed memories remain fully usable, and canonical machine-readable records never substitute a key for identity. The keyed JSON compatibility projection in R25 does not redefine canonical identity. _(S1, S2)_

**R3. Core fields describe portable Memory semantics; `metadata` is the extension point.** A core field holds only what is portable before an author knows how a memory will be used; a categorical field whose value would change with intended use is not core. Application-specific properties — ADR status, evidence, validity, confidence, context tier, a must-be-present marker, a class taxonomy — belong in the Bead's structured `metadata`, the extension point every Bead already carries. Metadata is part of durable Memory state: changing a key mints a version, it travels with the version, and — because versions are retained under policy — a value that must not persist does not belong in it. The Markdown body is content and carries no Bead properties. It may contain anything, including frontmatter and ordinary Markdown links to files, documents, websites, or other non-Bead resources; Beads preserves body content verbatim but does not interpret it, and never treats body text as Bead References or validates, synchronizes, authorizes, retargets, or promises the continued existence of link targets. Core Beads does not acquire each application's taxonomy.

Two core fields record a Memory's own derivation, because a record that dropped its evidence must not read like one that never had any. **Derived-from** is a core field, not a graph edge: a list of reference-shaped values — canonical ID and optional version — with three observable states: absent (a pre-schema or converted record; derivation unknown), an empty list (the author asserts the content directly — a deliberate value), or one or more entries (the tasks, documents, Memories, or external sources it was written from). **Derivation completeness** is a tri-state — complete, incomplete, or unknown — unknown for converted records and never defaulted. A Bead source is checkable by ordinary read; a non-Bead source is carried without validation, and completeness still distinguishes "source outside the graph" from "sources dropped at write time." Inception says how the record got into this store; the derivation record says what its content came from. _(S1, S6, S11, S14)_

**R4.** `bd remember` **is an explicit write.** It creates an unkeyed or keyed Memory Bead or updates an explicitly selected existing one. Positional text is body text, including a single token; stdin and file input use explicit forms. On creation, at least one of title or body contains non-whitespace content. When a non-empty body is supplied without a title, Beads derives a title; an empty body is valid when the caller supplies a non-empty title. Other omitted fields preserve current values. A successful `remember` result identifies the created or updated Memory — its canonical ID and title — so a write is always visibly a write. Beads never synthesizes a body from prompts, transcripts, tasks, tool activity, or search failure. _(S1, S2, S12)_

**R5. Deletion keeps history; erasure removes it.** `bd forget` and `bd delete` addressed to a Memory perform the same operation — a disappearance in the shared History sense: the current state is removed and the disappearance announced, key and aliases are released, and every retained version stays addressable under retention policy, so a read reports no current state and answers from history. Because history is not rewritten, deletion is reversible through the shared History capability R13 names: a restored Memory comes back under the same identity, and the restore reports the key unavailable rather than failing if a live Memory has since taken it. `forget` acts immediately because it is recoverable; `delete` keeps its shipped confirmation model — an unforced run previews, `--force` executes. A successful result says the Memory was deleted with its history retrievable subject to retention; it never implies erasure.

Erasure removes what must not exist. An erased version is removed, its address afterward answers gone with erasure as the reason (R16), and the removal is announced and propagated to every replica and cache holding it. Erasing one retained version is a shared History operation that never leaves a Memory without a current state; `bd delete --erase` erases every retained version and the identity with them, releases key and aliases, and requires `--force`. Erasure is irreversible: nothing restores the erased versions, their addresses, or the identity; content someone still holds can be re-recorded only as new versions at new addresses. _(S3, S15)_
### Recall and context consumers
**R6. Discovery is compact, deterministic, and honest about bounds.** `bd memories [search]` searches existing Memory Beads across key, aliases, title, and body. Results return in a documented deterministic order with stable positions — plain key or alphabetical order is an adequate contract — and relevance ranking is consumer-owned: conformance requires no full-text index, embeddings, persisted scores, or service. Ordinary and `--details` discovery returns each match once as a summary with canonical ID, title, an exact address for the selected state, bounded excerpt, optional key, match provenance, and continuation or completeness information, and an explicit control returns the complete result set rather than one page. An alias match identifies the matching alias. Continuation is bound to the original query and ordering; when relevant state may have changed, or on incompatible or expired reuse, it fails accurately rather than returning silently mixed, duplicated, or skipped results. Discovery never expands complete bodies; callers recall selected memories explicitly. _(S2, S4, S6, S12)_

**R7. Exact recall is complete and attributable.** `bd recall` returns one selected current or retained historical Memory state. Plain output contains the complete body without mixed diagnostics. Structured output keeps Project ID, Bead ID, key, complete alias set, Historical Bead Reference for the selected state, Change Attribution, Inception, derivation record, metadata, references, and complete body together. Memory presence is independent of body content: recalling an existing Memory with an empty body succeeds and returns that empty body, while an absent selector reports not found. Exact reads never silently truncate or substitute a different state. _(S4, S5, S6, S10)_

**R8. Retrieval is selective.** Task display, project initialization, `bd prime`, ordinary search, `--details`, and reference summaries never load Memory bodies automatically. Generated guidance tells agents to inspect references, search compact results, recall chosen bodies explicitly, search before writing, record only deliberately chosen durable knowledge, and keep short-lived progress or scratch state with the task or runtime. For each of those, the guidance shows the exact command to run, not a description of it. Those discovery paths never invoke explicit bulk compatibility projections. Generated guidance fits its surface's documented output budget and names which growing term that budget bounds; truncation is stated visibly to the reader and never recorded as complete delivery. _(S2, S4, S5, S12)_

**R9. Tasks expose references as structured data.** A task record reports Bead References, expected target kinds, the target information R20 requires, and any Historical Bead Reference separately from workflow dependencies and without expanding target bodies. The task body remains responsible for explaining why a reference matters. _(S5, S6, S9)_

**R10. Context consumers receive stable building blocks, not a core context-pack policy.** Structured Beads interfaces expose exact identities, historically addressed Memory states, Change Attribution, Inception, deterministic bounded traversal, and truthful completeness. Applications such as MindSpec own artifact schemas, required-versus-optional tiers, token counting, cross-source ordering, hashing, file snapshots, and receipt rendering. _(S6)_
### Shared versioning and history
**R11. Memory Beads participate in shared Beads History.** Every change to the durable Memory state the Core model enumerates creates a new version through Beads History. A request that leaves durable Memory state unchanged creates no version, even when the caller or other Change Attribution differs. Participation is unconditional: the Memory kind refuses a `storage_class: unversioned` marker at write time — typed and before mutation — rather than accepting a record whose marker the store would not honor. _(S1, S3, S7, S10)_

**R12. Change Attribution and Inception stay distinct.** Beads History associates Change Attribution with each accepted Memory version. Inception is editable Memory state. Changing Inception creates a version; changing only the caller or change context on an otherwise identical request does not. As Memory Capability Requirements on shared History, each accepted Memory version lets consumers obtain at least a responsible actor, an assisting agent when present, a timestamp, and a change message when present; richer attribution belongs to the shared History contract. Change Attribution alone does not claim that an identity was authenticated or authorized. _(S6, S7, S14)_

**R13. Memory exposes inherited history outcomes.** Shared Beads History lets callers view retained history, compare historical Memory states, inspect Change Attribution, cite an exact historical state, restore a deleted Memory's current state from a retained version — the latest by default, or a chosen one — as a new attributed version under the same identity, and find Memory Bead changes through the ordinary History query for all Bead changes in the project from a caller-held position — or from a caller-supplied instant on a first read, after which the position is the order. That change feed includes removals of retained versions with their reasons, so an application that mirrors Memory content can honor an erasure. The application consuming those changes owns any application-specific synchronization behavior. _(S5, S7, S10, S14, S16)_

**R14. Memory writes use the common Versioned Bead rules.** Retries, concurrent edits, stale-state handling, conflicts, and their results follow the same shared Versioned Bead contracts. Providers may impose documented finite limits; an oversized write fails before mutation. _(S7)_

**R15. Memory Beads requires the shared history capability.** Any Beads implementation advertising Memory Beads support supplies the Beads History capabilities Memory consumes. _(S7, S14)_

**R16. Retention is policy-dependent and removal is observable.** Availability follows an explicit user or provider retention policy governed by the shared Beads History contract. While a historical Memory state is retained, its specific version ID continues to resolve to exactly that state. When a state is removed, exact recall reports it gone with the reason — retention, erasure, or another disclosed reason — distinguishably from an identity that never existed, and never substitutes current content or rebinds the address. _(S3, S5, S10)_
### References
**R17. Bead References connect work and knowledge.** A Bead Reference is an explicit directional relationship. `related` is the built-in baseline this proposal's scenarios use, not a closed vocabulary: user-defined, non-workflow relationship types are first-class and may connect Task→Memory, Memory→Task, or Memory→Memory, with the type preserved verbatim whether or not the reading binary recognizes it. The boundary is workflow semantics: a relationship whose meaning depends on Task workflow — blocking readiness above all — cannot use a Memory endpoint; informational and user-defined types can. The shared graph owns declaration, validation, filtering, traversal, and, when available, federation of edge types; a type's meaning is its consumers', and can itself be recorded in a Memory Bead. A reference carries no prompt, trust, permission, or workflow effect, and prose never creates one implicitly. _(S5, S8)_

**R18. Every reference has a version.** A reference whose version is `latest` — the default when none is stated — follows its target's current state. A pinned reference, one whose version is a specific version ID, identifies one exact retained state, is valid only for a Bead participating in versioning, and resolves to exactly that state or to a typed refusal, never to a different state. Historical addressing is a shared Beads capability, not a Memory-only identifier. _(S5, S10)_

**R19. Memory references rely on validated shared-graph endpoints.** An accepted reference with a Memory endpoint identifies the intended live Beads and their expected kinds, and an exact target identifies a valid retained state. Invalid, self-referential, or ambiguous links fail before changing the Memory. A reference whose exact target this store cannot resolve is refused before mutation, and the refusal distinguishes three cases by type: an invalid selector; a target known to be gone; and a fully qualified target unresolved here, which a later sync may resolve. Repeating the same stored reference is a Memory no-op. Endpoint representation and validation mechanics belong to the shared graph contract. _(S8, S10)_

**R20. Target observations never rewrite the source.** Reading a reference truthfully reports whether the target resolves and, when it does, its kind-specific lifecycle. Deletion, restoration, or other target-state changes are reported separately from the stored reference. A surviving source keeps its reference without silently retargeting it or changing task readiness. Deleting a target neither preserves its content through the reference nor removes its retained versions: a pinned reference to one still resolves under the shared History contract. The shared Beads graph contract owns the observation vocabulary and representation; Memory requires only these observable outcomes. _(S9)_

**R21. References are neither instructions nor context expansion.** Creating, inspecting, or following a reference never loads a body recursively and grants nothing beyond its informational meaning. The source body explains intended use; the caller decides whether to read the target. _(S5, S8)_

**R22. Reference direction and completeness remain explicit.** A Memory stores its outgoing references as durable state, so adding, removing, or changing one versions that Memory and never versions the target. A version carries the Memory's whole outgoing reference set as it then stood, and that set shares the version's acceptance and retention fate; removing a reference creates a new source version without it, and every retained earlier version still carries it. Incoming views — cited-by among them — are computed views, never stored Memory state, and disclose whether bounded output is complete through the shared graph contract. _(S9, S10, S14)_

**R23. Shared link surfaces expose references without changing task workflow.** Today `bd link <source> <target> --type related` records the directional non-blocking `related` reference Memory uses; this proposal adds a new `bd unlink <source> <target>` command as its removal counterpart. A link with a Memory endpoint rejects blocking and other Task workflow dependency types. The shared graph contract owns the remaining command grammar and link-surface design. `bd show` reads a selected Bead, and `bd recall` reads current or historically addressed Memory content without recursive expansion. _(S8, S10, S12)_
### Compatibility and interchange
**R24. Legacy Memory conversion never claims false success.** Valid legacy key/value content can become canonical Memory Beads without silent loss. Conversion preserves keys, bodies, and any history or Inception that can be represented truthfully, and it does not invent unavailable historical authorship. A converted record's derivation record is absent and its completeness unknown (R3). A legacy key with an empty value is valid: conversion preserves the key, derives a title from it, and preserves the empty body. The accepted conversion change receives ordinary Change Attribution; absence of legacy authorship is disclosed rather than treated as missing Memory state. Ambiguity, identity or type collision, corruption, or credible loss stops with an actionable failure. Every currently supported way of storing or reaching legacy Memory data is accounted for so conversion cannot silently strand, duplicate, or split it; the broader compatibility policy decides whether a particular surface projects canonical Memory or is retired. Callers never receive a mixed or partially converted view presented as success. After interruption, they can use the unchanged legacy view or the complete canonical view, or inspect an unavailable conversion state with enough information to retry or recover. _(S11)_

**R25. Compatibility surfaces have explicit target meanings.** `remember`, `memories`, `recall`, and `forget` remain public entry points: `remember` writes, `forget` deletes without erasing history, canonical creation does not require or invent keys, and `prime` provides the selective-retrieval and deliberate-capture guidance in R8 without injecting bodies. Existing `bd memories --json` callers continue to receive a complete human-key-to-body map for canonical keyed Memory Beads until the broader Beads compatibility policy removes that contract. The map includes a real Memory keyed `schema_version`; the shipped collision that replaces its body with a schema-version number is a defect, not compatible behavior. The exact JSON envelope and transition mechanics belong to the broader structured-output compatibility policy. Existing supported keyed Go and HTTP Memory interfaces likewise remain complete-body projections of canonical keyed Memory Beads. Across the keyed CLI, Go, and HTTP projections, presence is independent of body content: an empty-body Memory is found, recalled, and deleted successfully, while an absent selector remains not found. Canonical structured discovery uses Bead IDs and includes unkeyed Memories through a separate representation. _(S12)_

**R26. One canonical core model serves every supported surface.** CLI commands, structured interfaces, HTTP handlers, embedded, proxied, and remote operation, conversion, interchange, and compatibility surfaces use the same Memory Beads semantics. A compatibility surface projects canonical Memory Beads and never creates or exposes a second key/value Memory store. A writer that cannot honor the store's canonical Memory model refuses before mutation; it never reports success for a write the canonical view will not carry. _(S11, S12, S14)_

**R27. Memory participates safely in shared interchange.** The shared Beads interchange capability can carry selected Memory state and Memory-related references while preserving their identity and meaning. A destination either publishes the connected Memory-containing unit or rejects it without partial success. It never identifies or retargets a Memory by a matching human key or a similar-looking destination ID. Formats, mappings, validation, publication, and treatment of deleted, omitted, or historical endpoints belong to the shared interchange, graph, and history contracts. No shipped interchange path satisfies this requirement today; connected-interchange conformance is not claimed until one does. _(S13)_

**R27a. Bulk exposure of Memory bodies is enumerated.** A projection surface is any operation returning Bead state beyond a single explicit read of one selected Bead — bulk and automatic export, interchange units, kind-agnostic listing, generated guidance. Every shipped projection surface declares one posture toward Memory Beads: **excluded** — no Memory rows; **summary** — canonical and Project IDs, key and aliases, title, addresses, Change Attribution, and at most R6's bounded excerpt, never a body and never metadata values; or **body-carrying** — complete records, metadata included, selected only by an explicit caller argument such as `--full`, never by stored configuration, which may narrow a surface toward excluded and nothing else. An unenumerated surface carries summary at most; a unit that merely references a Memory carries its summary; body-carrying output discloses that it carries bodies (a record-level kind marker suffices). The one exception is a provider-level whole-store backup whose stated purpose is restoring that store; a canonical export is never that backup. Changing a surface's posture is an R31 change. _(S3, S11, S13, S14)_
### Providers and ecosystem
**R28. Structured records support viewers and independent implementations.** Provider-independent records expose current and retained historical Memory state, existence or deletion, references, comparison, Change Attribution, and honest bounds through shared Beads semantics. _(S14)_

**R29. Deployment and governance do not change portable meaning.** Local or remote storage, single-user or multi-user operation, authentication, authorization, and governance are shared Beads concerns. Memory Beads defines no separate policy for them. Whatever facilities are present, portable Memory identity, content, lifecycle, and reference semantics stay the same. _(S14)_

**R30. Core preserves evidence; external tools judge quality.** Beads does not decide whether Memory content is true, fresh, useful, duplicated, contradictory, or applicable. It supplies bodies, Change Attribution, Inception, shared history, references, and structured interfaces so humans and specialized applications can make and explain those judgments. _(S2, S14)_
### Changes to `bd` commands
**R31. Every target addition or behavioral change to a `bd` command selected by this proposal is explicit and justified.** Against the pinned compatibility baseline in the Summary, the table below is exhaustive for command behavior this proposal selects; R25 defines the surviving compatibility meanings. Shared History and interchange command grammar remain outside this proposal. _(S1–S5, S8, S10, S12, S15)_

| Command | Today | Target | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bd remember` | A bare token matching an existing derived key reads it and reports a recall; an omitted key is invented from the content | Always writes — a single token is body text; never invents a key; success output names the created or updated Memory | Store-state-dependent reads and writes under one verb caused ambiguity and previously led to silent overwrites and junk keys; write-only behavior with a visible success result removes that ambiguity, and canonical identity makes invented keys unnecessary |
| `bd recall` | Key-addressed; a stored empty value is indistinguishable from absence | Selects by canonical ID or key; presence is independent of body content; reads exact historical states | The empty-equals-absent conflation leaves recall and forget unable to manage an empty row; historical reads let a task cite the exact knowledge it used |
| `bd memories` | Lists or searches the key/value set; `--json` silently replaces the body of a memory keyed `schema_version` with the schema-version number | Compact bounded summaries with honest completeness over existing memories, in a documented deterministic order; the `--json` map stays complete, including a real memory keyed `schema_version`, and is body-carrying by contract (R25), named as such under R27a | Discovery must stay cheap enough that agents search before writing or bulk-reading; the key collision silently corrupted output — a defect, not compatible behavior |
| `bd forget` | Hard-deletes a found non-empty entry; out-of-band empty rows survive and need recovery | Deletes the Memory per R5 — a disappearance with every retained version still addressable — immediately, because it is recoverable; works for any present Memory | Current deletion loses the record; a disappearance removes the entry and keeps the history, and presence-independence eliminates the stuck-empty-row class |
| `bd delete` | Deletes issues and cleans up references; an unforced run behaves as a dry-run and `--force` confirms | For a Memory, the same disappearance as `forget` under the shipped preview-unless-`--force` model; `--erase` (requires `--force`) erases the whole Bead per R5 | Delete disappears without rewriting history; erase removes history for content that must not exist — two operations the shared History model already distinguishes, and Memory must not fuse them |
| `bd prime` | Injects memory bodies at session start and supports optional count and byte caps | Injects no bodies; generated guidance teaches selective search, explicit recall, and deliberate capture | Injection spends context before the agent knows what it needs and grows with the corpus; selective retrieval scales with it |
| `bd link` | Records a dependency between issues, defaulting to blocking; `--type related` already creates a non-blocking relationship | `--type related` and user-defined non-workflow types accept Memory endpoints; a link with a Memory endpoint rejects blocking and other Task workflow dependency types | Knowledge must never gate readiness; a default-blocking edge to a Memory would turn knowledge into workflow |
| `bd unlink` (new) | Does not exist | Removes the reference `bd link` records; removing a Memory's outgoing reference versions the source, never the target | `bd link` has no link-level removal counterpart, and reference removal is a durable change to the source Memory |
| `bd list` | Lists records from the Task-oriented issue model | Generic listing by kind can include `type: memory`; Task-workflow filters do not select Memories; Memory rows are summary per R27a | Memory is a peer core Bead kind but has no Task workflow state |
| `bd show` | Reads Task-oriented issue records | Reads a selected Task or Memory Bead and exposes its identity and references without recursively expanding referenced bodies | Humans and tools need one generic Bead inspection surface without turning a reference into implicit context loading |
| `bd graph` and other generic graph traversal | Traverse the Task-oriented issue graph | Can include Memory nodes and informational references without loading bodies or changing readiness; Memory nodes are summary per R27a | Memory is a first-class graph node, while its references remain informational |
| `bd export`, automatic export, `bd backup` | Export issues to JSONL and back up the database, with no stated Memory posture | Each declares its R27a posture; body-carrying only by explicit caller argument; a provider-level whole-store backup is R27a's stated exception | Bulk surfaces are where silent body exposure would hide; R27a makes each posture a stated choice rather than an inheritance |
| Any command or query whose meaning requires Task workflow state | Operates on the existing Task-oriented issue model, which has no first-class Memory kind | Does not select or affect Memory Beads; a workflow mutation explicitly addressed to one fails with a typed error | Memory is knowledge rather than work and must not acquire readiness, assignment, claiming, priority, completion, closure, or blocking semantics |

## Technical considerations
### TC1. Memory rests on shared Beads capabilities
Memory Beads belongs in Beads' core domain beside Task Beads. It must use canonical Bead identity and shared graph and history capabilities without inheriting task workflow fields. Its public semantics remain consistent across supported access modes.

Memory states what it needs from each required shared capability as Memory Capability Requirements — observable outcomes at the Memory boundary — without defining any capability's general contract. This map names each required capability and the requirements that state Memory's demands on it:

| Required shared capability | Memory's demands |
| --- | --- |
| Canonical identity and kind dispatch | R1–R3 |
| Beads History and Versioned Bead | R4, R5, R7, R9–R16, R28 |
| Shared graph: references, endpoint validation, and truthful target information | R17–R23 |
| Shared graph: complete predicate-filtered incoming lookup at a Memory endpoint | R20, R22 |
| Discovery continuation with accurate invalidation | R6  |
| Shared interchange | R27 |
| Compatibility baseline | R24–R26, R31, TC6–TC7 |

Optional capabilities — not required for conformance — compose with Memory: a shared Preview or dry-run capability, governance and authentication, deployment topology (R29), and cross-project reference identity and resolution under federation. Concerns this proposal deliberately does not own are grouped under Out of scope.
### TC2. Memory relies on shared Beads History
Memory Beads is a Versioned Bead kind; R15 conditions advertising Memory support on the History capabilities Memory requires. The shared Beads History and Versioned Bead contracts govern history identifiers, retention, compaction, writes, retries, concurrent edits, conflicts, comparisons, and Change Attribution; defining those contracts is outside this proposal, and R16 states Memory's retention and removal demands. Current-state selection is not a history operation: a Bead's current state is whatever its ordinary read means, and Memory requires only that the version the current state was accepted from be identifiable. Branches are outside Memory's demands — no Memory requirement consumes them. Dolt is one possible implementation, not the portable Memory model.
### TC3. Bead References use the shared graph
Memory Beads needs tasks to cite knowledge and memories to cite supporting knowledge, but it does not redefine task workflow. The shared graph owns endpoint and relationship behavior, the general link surface (R23 adds only `bd unlink`), and the representation and vocabulary used to report target information. Memory references introduce no new built-in edge kind: `related` is the baseline, and user-defined non-workflow types are first-class on Memory endpoints (R17). Other Memory-specific requirements are limited to keeping target bodies out of reference views, requiring truthful resolution and lifecycle information, and treating outgoing references as part of a Memory Bead's durable state.

Changing an outgoing reference changes the source. It creates a new version only when the source is a Versioned Bead and never versions the target. Historical Bead References and observations of deleted or missing targets use shared Beads history and graph behavior rather than Memory-specific representations.

One confirmed implementation note: today's `dependencies` table constrains sources to `issues`, and its target foreign key cascades on delete (migration 0041), so a reference that must survive its target — and retained versions that must keep their reference sets — require changing that mechanism. A tracker item, not a contract concern.
### TC4. Memory depends on identity-aware shared interchange
Project and Bead identity remain part of canonical Memory state; R27 defines the connected-unit and identity rules. This proposal does not define interchange formats, identity mappings, transaction mechanics, historical backup, synchronization, or physical encoding.
### TC5. Search, recall, and context assembly are separate operations
Discovery must stay compact enough that agents use it before writing or bulk-reading; R6–R9 and R21 bind the split — compact search, complete recall, body-free reference display, nothing recursive. Memory does not require snapshot isolation across discovery calls.

MindSpec supplies useful evidence for the consumer side of this split. Its context builder orders Bead JSON, specs, ADRs, plans, domain documents, and file inputs, then applies its own deterministic budget and hashing policy. Those choices belong to the consumer because another application will have different artifact types and priorities. Memory Beads supplies exact, attributable, versioned knowledge inputs without owning context-pack policy. The [MindSpec architecture description](https://github.com/mrmaxsteel/mindspec/blob/09f62bd97b28bae7b171054066117cb19a33874d/.mindspec/core/ARCHITECTURE.md) documents that source model, while its pinned [budgeter specification](https://github.com/mrmaxsteel/mindspec/blob/09f62bd97b28bae7b171054066117cb19a33874d/.mindspec/specs/088-context-pack-budgeter/spec.md#L246-L355) records its ordering, budgeting, and receipt behavior.
### TC6. Compatibility surfaces project canonical Memory Beads
Every compatibility surface is a projection of the same canonical Memory Beads (R26), R25 itemizes each entry point's target meaning, and R31 records each change from today's behavior with its rationale. One behavior deserves its own callout: `bd remember` only writes, so every positional argument accepted as content — including a single token — is stored as body text; it never reads. R24's universal accounting rule covers every other currently supported way of storing or reaching legacy Memory data without turning this proposal into an API inventory.

One shipped hazard is recorded for the tracker rather than this contract: `BD_IGNORE_SCHEMA_SKEW=1` currently downgrades the forward-drift refusal to a warning on writable opens, which is exactly the stranded-write path R26 forbids.
### TC7. Legacy conversion is governed by observable safety
R24 states the observable safety contract. The implementation must account for every supported legacy view and stop when it cannot convert that state truthfully. Empty legacy values are representable canonical Memory state, not a conversion failure. Scanning, staging, atomic-switch, recovery-command, and rollout mechanisms are implementation concerns, not requirements of this proposal.
### TC8. Structured output is the ecosystem seam
Viewer, context, conversion, and quality tools should not read provider tables; public structured records preserve the fields R7 and R28 enumerate. Schemas fail closed when a client cannot preserve required semantics.

Stored titles, excerpts, bodies, and provider diagnostics are untrusted input. Human renderers prevent content from masquerading as terminal diagnostics, and structured renderers escape it correctly. These protections make external analysis safer without giving Beads an opinion about whether the content itself is good.

## Out of scope
### Definitions Memory requires but does not own
These are required shared capabilities from the TC1 map whose general contracts are defined outside this proposal; Memory states only its demands on them.

- Defining the general Beads History or Versioned Bead contracts; TC2 enumerates their concerns.
  
- Choosing internal package or interface boundaries, storage schemas, migration algorithms, or provider mechanisms.
  
- Setting a universal history-retention duration or defining provider-specific compaction, hard-erasure, legal-hold, or unavailable-history mechanisms. Those belong to user policy and shared Beads History contracts; exactness and accurate unavailability at the Memory boundary remain in scope.
  
### Optional capabilities Memory composes with when present
These are not required for Memory Beads conformance; when Beads provides one, Memory participates under its shared contract without a Memory-specific variant.

- When federation (cross-project linking) is available, Memory Beads works with it.
  
- Defining a Memory-specific preview or dry-run protocol. When Beads provides a shared Preview capability, Memory participates under its rules.
  
- Requiring local or remote storage, a single- or multi-user topology, verified identity, RBAC, per-Memory secrecy, mandatory review, or one portable remote role ladder.
  
### Never in scope
- Choosing Dolt or any other storage provider or storage-specific realization of Beads History.
  
- Defining implementation sequencing, feature flags, rollout strategy, release timing, migration procedure, or deprecation schedules.
  
- Automatically creating memories from prompts, transcripts, tasks, tool activity, or search failure.
  
- Automatically loading every memory, every linked body, or a transitive reference graph into agent context.
  
- Granting read, write, tool, or delegation authority because a Memory Bead or Bead Reference says so.
  
- Making any application taxonomy — ADR status, validity, confidence, context tier, class, supersession — a universal core field; those live in `metadata` (R3).
  
- An archive or any other soft lifecycle state in core: a Memory exists, has been deleted with its history retained, or has been erased.
  
- Judging truth, freshness, duplication, contradiction, usefulness, or applicability in core Beads.
  
- Building a general document database, attachment store, rich wiki renderer, or real-time collaborative editor.
  
- Treating canonical import or export as historical backup or synchronization.
  
- Shipping an official Memory viewer; supported structured interfaces are the product boundary for viewers.
